To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
spatially controlled switching of AMPAR properties in the forebrain leads to enhanced olfactory discrimination, but impaired olfactory memory.

1) the switch of AMPARs from Ca2+-impermeable to Ca2+-per-meable, by spatially restricted genetic manipulations, leads to enhanced olfactory discrimination but impaired olfactory memory; 2) the switch of GluR subunit composition from GluR-B to GluR-B/Q in forebrain is variable among individuals, and the variability is strongly correlated to olfactory memory impairment; 3) the olfactory discrimination is enhanced independently of
the spatially controlled switch of the Ca2+-permanence of AMPA-type glutamate receptor (AMPARs), in mice forebrain, enhances odor discrimination and impairs olfactory memory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms of olfactory behavior and memory.
the role of AMPARs in learning and memory.
the role of AMPA receptors in olfactory learning and memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spatial switch of AMPARs in the forebrain of mice leads to enhanced olfactory discrimination but impairs olfactory memory.
the spatially controlled switch of AMPARs is an efficient and effective tool to dissect molecular mechanisms underlying olfactory behavior.
GluR-B is not essential for learning and memory but that the expression of the GluA1 subunit is required for the acquisition and consolidation of olfactory memories in the mouse.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatially and temporally controlled switch of the Ca2+ permeable AMPA receptor in forebrain is sufficient to enhance odor discrimination and impair olfactory memory.
Ca2+-permissive AMPARs are required for odor learning and memory in the olfactory system, but are dispensable for odor discrimination.
the Ca2+-per-meable AMPAR switch in the forebrain is a key molecular mechanism for olfactory memory.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the same molecular modification can have opposite effects in distinct brain circuits.
spatially controlled switch of AMPARs in forebrain can be a useful approach to dissect molecular mechanisms underlying olfactory discrimination and olfactory memory.
spatially controlled switch of AMPARs can be used to study the molecular mechanisms of sensory perception, memory, and learning.
